scenario: Today's systems track is about caching and queueing. Fairway, Penelope and a paper on agent serving that cannot recover after a traffic surge all ask the same kind of question. Once prefix caches are heavily reused, which request should run first, which segment should be evicted, and when should fewer new sessions be admitted? AttentionIndex speeds up the token-picking step of sparse attention by treating it as a nearest-neighbor search, and OctEx spends GPU memory to remove the round-after-round waiting in vector search. Scute lets one GPU serve many kinds of fine-tuning adapters in one batch. On the engineering side, there is low-bit quantized storage in Qdrant, prefix-aware routing in SageMaker, automatic training recovery from NVIDIA, and Google's experience hunting XLA compiler bugs.

papers.title: Fairway: Load-Aware KV Cache Reuse for LLM Prefill Scheduling
papers.authors: Hamidreza Alikhani, Nazmul Takbir, Matin Khajavi, Rajat Bhattacharjya, Sangeetha Abdu Jyothi, Nikil Dutt
papers.abstract: LLM-based applications often employ agentic workflows and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which build long prompts from shared context. When prefixes are shared across requests, serving engines reuse the key-value (KV) cache to skip parts of the prefill computation. Reuse is typically graded: the uncached work of requests in a queue can differ by up to 100x. In this setting, the order of scheduling determines the time-to-first-token (TTFT) for the queued requests. KV reuse-first scheduling, which prioritizes the requests with the longest KV cache hit, gives the lowest median TTFT but starves expensive requests under load spikes; first-come-first-served (FCFS) scheduling bounds the tail but raises the median TTFT. We present Fairway, a prefill scheduler built on adaptive reuse prioritization: it favors KV cache reuse while queues are short, and shifts toward fair allocation as requests wait longer relative to their own prefill time. Fairway employs a virtual dual lane model: a KV reuse-first Fast lane and a Fair lane atop the serving engine's waiting queue that enables speeding up of cheap reuse requests without starving expensive ones. This model automatically adapts to the workload without any per-workload tuning. Fairway lowers the tail TTFT at no cost to the median in transient overload. Across workloads and load levels, Fairway matches or beats the best baseline, with a p99 TTFT up to 8.6x lower than prior prefix-aware schedulers. During load spikes, it keeps the tail of FCFS at a 6x lower median TTFT.
papers.summary: Prefill queueing under a prefix cache can keep both the median latency low and the tail short. While the queue is short, serve cheap requests with long cache hits first; move a request forward the longer it has waited relative to its own prefill time; and cap how much work cheap requests may place ahead of the oldest request. This is what Fairway does. Agent and RAG requests often share a prefix, so the remaining work of requests in one queue can differ by about 100 times, and the serving order decides how long each request waits for its first token. In traffic spikes, Fairway's median time to first token is 0.82 seconds with a p99 close to first-come-first-served, while hit-leaning orderings let the p99 reach 11 to 50 seconds.

deep_reading.title: Fairway: Load-Aware KV Cache Reuse for LLM Prefill Scheduling

papers.title: AttentionIndex: Accelerating Learned Sparse Attention with a Causal Inverted-File Index
papers.abstract: Learned sparse attention, used in production models such as DeepSeek-V4 and GLM-5, lets each query attend to only k keys chosen by a lightweight indexer, but the indexer still scores every key in the prefix. At one million tokens, this selection takes more than half of prefill time. Two-stage selection over contiguous blocks, as in HiSA, reduces this cost, but its recall declines as context grows at a fixed candidate budget. We present AttentionIndex, which routes each query over an inverted-file index that groups indexer keys by similarity and refines the candidates with the native indexer score. AttentionIndex builds the index during prefill, making new keys searchable immediately, reusing previous clustering to keep maintenance cheap, and exposing each query only to clusters built from its own prefix. On GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at one million tokens, AttentionIndex delivers 1.3-1.8 times the prefill throughput of exhaustive selection, and at throughput within 5% of HiSA, it recovers 17.0 and 10.0 percentage points more of the exhaustive top-k, respectively. AttentionIndex also improves accuracy on long-context benchmarks by up to 18.4 percentage points over HiSA at the same candidate budget.
papers.summary: In learned sparse attention, as used by DeepSeek-V4 and GLM-5.3, each query attends to only k keys, but the small scoring network that picks those k keys still scores every key in the prefix. At one million tokens, that step takes more than half of prefill time. AttentionIndex sharply cuts this cost. During prefill it groups keys by similarity; a query first scores one representative per group, and only the members of the most promising groups go to the original scoring network for the final pick. At that length, its prefill throughput is 1.3 to 1.8 times that of scoring every key, and it misses fewer keys than HiSA, a block-based method at similar speed.

deep_reading.title: AttentionIndex: Accelerating Learned Sparse Attention with a Causal Inverted-File Index

papers.title: When Cache Pressure Becomes a Trap: Metastability in Agent Serving
papers.authors: Chengzhi Lu, Boxi Zhou, Yanying Lin, Dmitrii Ustiugov
papers.abstract: LLM agents repeatedly send a growing conversation to a model, making prefix reuse central to efficient serving. We show that a brief surge can disrupt this reuse and trigger metastable failure in prefill--decode (PD) disaggregated engines: service remains degraded after arrivals return to a load the engine previously sustained. On SGLang, a ten-minute surge reduced goodput by about 88% over the following hour. Removing the residual burst sessions restored service within minutes. The sustaining mechanism is population-cache feedback. Slower calls prolong sessions and enlarge their aggregate context, or working set; the resulting cache misses increase recomputation and further delay departures. A fluid model identifies the resource conditions for this feedback and explains how cache capacity, tool time and base load affect vulnerability. Across 36 simulated deployments, it flags all 17 cache-first cases. Controlled simulations hold the post-surge state fixed and show that changing subsequent arrivals alone reverses the recovery outcome. Once the cache collapses, low-reuse departure capacity sets the scale of the load reduction needed for recovery. Guided by these dynamics, we build Basin, which gives each session a fixed priority, reserves their predicted peak contexts against an adaptive admission budget, extends the cache with idle decode memory, and sheds excess demand. On real H200 1P3D deployments under surges, including long-context SWE-bench Pro sessions, an arrival-time prototype achieves 1.20--1.70x the goodput of Continuum and 2.35--3.59x that of HiCache alone. In simulation, the predictor-driven policy delivers 1.20--2.05x the strongest baseline's goodput across six surge scenarios.
papers.summary: A ten-minute traffic surge can leave an agent serving engine with prefill and decode disaggregated unable to recover. After the surge ends and traffic returns to a level the engine handled before, goodput on SGLang stays about 88% lower over the following hour, and ==utilization and queue length give almost no warning beforehand.== Behind it is a loop: too little cache causes recomputation, calls slow down, sessions end later, more context is live at once, and the cache falls even shorter. Based on this, the authors build Basin. It reserves each session's predicted largest context from a total budget and queues new sessions when the budget runs out. On real GPUs, a simplified prototype without the predictor already reaches 1.20 to 1.70 times the goodput of Continuum, the strongest prior system.

deep_reading.title: When Cache Pressure Becomes a Trap: Metastability in Agent Serving

papers.title: OctEx: Billion-Scale Vector Search by Precomputed Lattice Neighbor Lists on GPUs
papers.abstract: Approximate nearest-neighbor search on GPUs serves retrieval-augmented generation, recommendation, and deduplication over datasets of up to billions of vectors. The fastest GPU indexes at high recall, such as CAGRA, walk proximity graphs in chained rounds, each of which waits for the distances of the previous one. High recall therefore costs many dependent rounds per query. Our insight is to spend the HBM of the GPUs on precomputed neighbor lists, so that a query reads its candidates in one parallel step instead of a chain of rounds. This paper turns the above insight into a GPU vector search system, namely OctEx, which holds hundreds of randomly projected copies of the dataset in GPU memory. Every copy rounds its vectors to the nearest points of a regular grid whose cells are nearly round and stores for every populated cell the list of vectors nearest to its center. A query reads the lists of its cells in all copies at once and then, in a fixed number of waves, the precomputed neighbor lists of its best hits. OctEx ranks the union of all hits by an int8 sketch before one exact rerank. OctEx runs the whole search of a batch as CUDA graphs over all GPUs of a server and places every part of its index in HBM or host memory by its access frequency. On four H100 GPUs at recall 0.95 to 0.995, OctEx outperforms CAGRA by 2.0x to 46.4x on seven datasets of up to one hundred million vectors, and by 1.46x to 2.05x on the one billion vectors of Deep1B and SIFT1B, whose indexes it builds in 44 to 47 minutes. OctEx also outperforms GGNN, PathWeaver, FlowANN, and the cuVS inverted file indexes IVF-PQ and IVF-RaBitQ by 5.4x to 343x.
papers.summary: For high-recall vector search on GPUs, graph search is held back by its chain of dependent rounds, not by distance computation itself. OctEx spends GPU memory on neighbor lists precomputed at build time. It makes a few hundred randomly projected low-dimensional copies of the data, cuts each copy into grid cells, and stores for every cell a list of the vectors closest to its center. A query computes which cell it falls into in each copy, reads those lists in one parallel step to get candidates, then reads the stored neighbor tables of the best few candidates for a fixed few rounds. Against CAGRA, the standard GPU graph-search baseline, it is 2.0 to 46.4 times faster at high recall on seven datasets of up to one hundred million vectors. On billion-vector datasets, the gain shrinks to 1.46 to 2.05 times. ==Trading GPU memory for serial waiting at query time is the core trade-off of this paper.==

deep_reading.title: OctEx: Billion-Scale Vector Search by Precomputed Lattice Neighbor Lists on GPUs

papers.title: Rethinking KV Cache Eviction for Agentic LLM Serving
papers.authors: Jiakun Fan, Han Meng, Yuxuan Xia, Hao Mark Chen, Dong Li, Dimitrios S. Nikolopoulos
papers.abstract: Key-value (KV) caches impose substantial memory pressure on large language model serving systems, requiring cache eviction when capacity is insufficient. Existing mechanisms typically evict KV from the ends of cached sequences to preserve prefix sharing across requests. However, agent workloads repeatedly reuse long histories across successive turns. Recomputing the KV cache for tokens near the end of a sequence is substantially more expensive than for earlier tokens because their attention computation involves longer histories. To address this problem, we propose preserving shared prefixes and evicting the KV cache from the beginning of the remaining history while retaining the cached suffix. We build Penelope around this strategy by co-designing the eviction policy, KV recomputation, and unified GPU-CPU cache management. Returning requests reuse the KV cache retained in GPU or CPU memory and recompute only missing segments while preserving reuse of the cached suffix. We implement Penelope in SGLang and evaluate it on three Qwen3 model sizes using real agent traces. Compared with SGLang, Penelope reduces mean time to first token by up to 60% and job completion time by up to 37% with a GPU-only cache, and by up to 76% and 60% with a two-tier GPU-CPU cache.
papers.summary: When the KV cache runs out of room, vLLM and SGLang both evict from the end of cached sequences, to keep the opening prefix that many requests can share. But an agent sends its long history back every turn, and later tokens cost more to recompute, because each attends to every token before it. Penelope does the opposite: it still keeps the shared prefix, but evicts the rest of the history from the front and keeps the later part. When the request returns, only the missing segment is recomputed. On SGLang with real agent traces, mean time to first token drops by up to 60% with a GPU-only cache, and by up to 76% with CPU memory added as a second cache tier. ==Which segment to evict should depend on how much it costs to recompute, not only on how many requests share it.==

deep_reading.title: Rethinking KV Cache Eviction for Agentic LLM Serving

papers.title: Scute: Exact Batched Serving for PEFT Adapters Beyond LoRA
papers.abstract: Existing serving systems for large language models batch requests for many different LoRA adapters on one GPU. However, these systems reject adapters from other parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as DoRA, (IA), VeRA and OFT. One solution to this is to convert these adapters to LoRA, but this induces a significant memory and accuracy cost. Instead, we show that, under some modifications, a batched LoRA kernel can serve all of these methods exactly and efficiently. We achieve this by writing each method in one normal form, a LoRA computation with six slots for an adapter's own vectors and matrices. Some slots can merge into an adapter's weights at load time; the others remain live and induce a cost. We give ways to efficiently pay this cost and predict it from a zero-parameter byte model. We package this system, Scute, and build it on top of vLLM. Scute serves all five methods, coming as checkpoints from the Hugging Face PEFT library, in one batch, and it matches that library with a mean error of at most 1.5% of each adapter's effect. Under a burst of requests on an RTX A6000, a mix of these methods takes 5-17% more decode time than the same number of LoRA adapters. Furthermore, using Scute, the same GPU can serve 64 to 1024 (IA) and VeRA adapters at 1.5x to at least 2.5x the request rate of their LoRA conversions.
papers.summary: With a few changes, vLLM's existing batched LoRA kernel can run adapters trained with DoRA, (IA)³, VeRA and OFT exactly, in the same batch as LoRA adapters, without converting them to LoRA first. The method sets aside a few places in the LoRA computation, such as rotating the input before the base weight or multiplying each output column by a factor, and each adapter fills them with its own vectors or matrices. When the matrix next to a place belongs to the adapter, the vector is multiplied into that matrix once at load and costs nothing while serving; when only the shared base weight sits next to it, it is computed at every step. On one RTX A6000, a mix of four or five methods takes only 5% to 17% more decode time than the same number of plain LoRA adapters. ==Exact serving itself costs little extra time, and it avoids the accuracy loss and memory of conversion.==

deep_reading.title: Scute: Exact Batched Serving for PEFT Adapters Beyond LoRA

papers.title: Faster and Cheaper Search With Qdrant 1.20
papers.abstract:
With Qdrant 1.20, we shipped two main features that can make your search cheaper and faster: two new quantization-native datatypes (turbo8 and turbo16) and advanced metadata indexing for nested fields. We measured the performance and cost improvements so you don’t have to, and in this blog post we go through our findings.

Reduce Your Disk Usage, Not Your Recall

Storing vectors is always the main expense when it comes to semantic search: they cost disk when cold, and memory when warm.
papers.summary: In a vector database, the biggest cost is often storing the vectors themselves: disk when cold and memory when warm. Qdrant 1.20 adds two low-bit storage types, turbo8 and turbo16. Rather than simply cutting float32 down to lower precision, they rotate each vector first and then quantize it, which keeps more of the information search needs. On a test set of vectors from the Qdrant team, turbo8 takes a quarter of the space of float32 with slightly higher recall, and server-side latency is less than 10% higher than with float32. Latency grows little because the query vector is only rotated, not quantized. ==Rotating before quantizing saves space while keeping recall almost unchanged.==

papers.title: XLA from the Trenches: Correctness on TPU Workloads at Scale
papers.authors: Ignacio Cano, Amir Saadat, Rishipal Singh Bhatia, Samuel Ginzburg, Patrick C. Toulme, Ioannis Zarkadas, Praveen Narayanan, Pratik Bhatu, Nicolas Basile, Alexander Dietmüller, Ruishan Wang, Jacob Wahlgren, Victor Barros, Subhankar Shah, Michael Kuperstein, Farzin Houshmand, Emma Sevastian, Peter Gavin, Karthik Srinivasa Murthy, Berkin Ilbeyi, Amit Sabne, Eli Bendersky
papers.abstract: Accelerating modern foundational models has pushed domain-specific compilers toward increasingly complex, multi-tiered optimization pipelines. However, this heavy optimization focus introduces delicate tradeoffs between peak execution performance and correctness. Subtle codegen defects can trigger numerical degradation and memory or buffer corruption, invalidating multi-million-dollar training runs and degrading live serving quality without raising obvious compiler errors. In this paper, we present a battle-tested methodology for verifying and triaging Google's XLA:TPU compiler at hyperscale. We leverage fuzzing techniques, combining synthetic program generation with real production traces, while orchestrating AI agent swarms to autonomously generate stress tests, reproduce failures, and draft fixes. To pinpoint root causes in full workloads, we pair this with a hierarchical differential pipeline that bisects large graphs down to individual failing operations inside fused kernels. Deployed in production, our framework has already driven the resolution of over 142 compiler bugs (with 103 additional findings under review), from which we distill pragmatic lessons learned.
papers.summary: A compiler bug may raise no error at all and just shift the numbers quietly, making an expensive training run diverge weeks later or degrading live inference quality. Google describes how they hunt such problems in the XLA compiler for TPUs at scale. On one side, they fuzz with randomly generated programs and real production graphs, and let a swarm of AI agents write stress tests, reproduce failures and draft fixes. On the other side, to locate a fault they bisect the failing large graph step by step, down to the single failing operation inside a fused kernel. Since deployment, the process has driven fixes for more than 142 compiler bugs, with 103 more findings under review. ==Compiler correctness needs continuous production-scale testing, and regression suites alone fall far short.==

papers.title: Keep Distributed Training Running with Automated Workload Recovery
papers.abstract: As distributed AI training scales, failures across hardware and software dependencies increasingly disrupt training progress, making fast, reliable recovery...
papers.summary: The larger distributed training gets, the more often a training process stalls, a node stops responding or one machine slows the whole job. Each time someone has to read logs, find the bad node and restart from a checkpoint, while the GPUs sit idle. NVIDIA's open-source NVIDIA Recovery automates this: it detects anomalies from application logs, GPU metrics and scheduler signals, works out which machine is at fault, isolates it, and restarts or stops the job according to policy. New deployments only make recommendations by default and take no action, so operators can first confirm the signals are reliable. Over three months on a training cluster running about 200 jobs a day, it detected anomalies in 69 seconds on average and took recovery action in 94 seconds. ==Starting with recommendations only and then turning on automatic action makes such a system much less risky to roll out.==

papers.title: Reduce LLM latency with prefix-aware routing on Amazon SageMaker Inference
papers.authors: Kareem Syed-Mohammed, Dmitry Soldatkin, Vamsi Goparaju, Vivek Gangasani, Xu Deng, Xiaoguang Chen
papers.abstract: When you build an application on top of a large language model (LLM), the prompt you send to the model typically has two parts. There’s a fixed part that sets up context (instructions, reference documents, conversation history) and a variable part that contains the actual user input.
papers.summary: Many LLM applications start their prompts with a large fixed block, such as a few thousand tokens of support rules, followed by one line from the user. Prefix caching on a single machine skips recomputing that block, but with many machines requests are spread at random, each one rarely sees the same opening twice, and the cache is barely used. Amazon SageMaker's new prefix-aware routing sends requests with the same opening to the same machine. When that machine is full, the request goes to an idle one instead, and scaling up or down moves only a small share of traffic. In AWS benchmarks, the cache hit rate rose from about 25% to over 80%, and median time to first token fell by up to 77%. ==With many instances, whether prefix caching pays off depends on routing.==
